formality: Informal 'você' address throughout the UI (never 'tu', never formal 'o(a) senhor(a)') — the standard register for Brazilian SaaS/security tooling: direct, professional, not stiff.
styleNotes: Use Brazilian vocabulary and spelling, not European Portuguese (arquivo not ficheiro, senha not palavra-passe, tela not ecrã). Address the user as 'você'. Keep hashcat/infosec loanwords that are already standard in the BR community in English rather than forcing a literal translation (see keepEnglish:true terms below) — but don't over-apply this to generic English words that do translate naturally. Prefer plain, concrete technical Portuguese over a formal/academic register (e.g. 'limite' over 'limiar', 'excedente' over 'transbordamento') so copy reads like a security tool, not a textbook.

hash.note: Standard term in security tools and documentation; universally used in Portuguese security community

hashlist.note: Product concept; kept as brand terminology, consistent with hash/wordlist/potfile staying English

crack.note: Standard Portuguese verb in security contexts; 'crackear' also used colloquially but 'quebrar' is more formal

cracked.note: Adjective form; feminine form is 'quebrada' (for feminine nouns like 'senha')

plaintext.note: Standard terminology in Microsoft/Windows security documentation

potfile.note: hashcat-specific filename; kept as technical term

wordlist.note: Common in hashcat documentation; some contexts use 'lista de palavras' but 'wordlist' is industry standard

mask.note: Standard term in Portuguese hashcat documentation

charset.note: hashcat parameter term; used as-is in security tools; could also be 'conjunto de caracteres' but 'charset' is preferred in technical contexts

brute force.note: Standard Portuguese term across security industry

keyspace.note: Commonly kept in hashcat context; technical term used in security documentation; 'espaço de chaves' is literal but 'keyspace' is industry standard

effective keyspace.note: First word kept as 'keyspace'; 'efetivo' is the translation

chunk.note: Fixed from draft's 'fragmento': 'bloco' is the standard Portuguese term for a contiguous unit of work/data (cf. 'processamento em blocos'); 'fragmento' wrongly suggests something broken or incomplete, which isn't the intended meaning here

job.note: Fixed from draft's 'trabalho': 'job' is the core scheduling concept in distributed-computing/cracking tools (Kubernetes Jobs, Jenkins, cron) and is kept untranslated by Brazilian infosec/sysadmin usage; 'trabalho' loses the specific technical sense and reads like generic 'work'

preset job.note: First word kept as 'job' (see job); 'predefinido' is the translation, matching the 'effective keyspace' pattern

loopback.note: Technical term; could be 'realimentação' but 'loopback' is understood in security contexts

overflow.note: Fixed from draft's 'transbordamento': this means extra/excess agents beyond a job's limit, not liquid overflowing a container; 'excedente' (surplus) is the natural, precise term for scheduler/allocation contexts

benchmark.note: hashcat term; universal in Portuguese security industry

claim code.note: Fixed from draft's 'código de reivindicação': 'reivindicação' is a legal-claim register (labor/property claims) that doesn't fit a registration code; 'registro' matches the actual action of claiming/registering an agent

voucher.note: Fixed from draft's 'comprovante': 'voucher' is an established loanword in Brazilian Portuguese (gift/travel/promo vouchers) and matches the product's own English UI noun (admins generate 'vouchers'); 'comprovante' wrongly suggests a payment receipt

heartbeat.note: Fixed from draft's 'batida de coração': 'heartbeat' is the universal term for periodic check-in signals in Brazilian Portuguese infra/SRE writing; the literal translation reads like a human heartbeat and sounds unnatural in a monitoring UI

offline buffer.note: Could also be 'buffer offline' but 'período de graça' better conveys the grace period concept

archive.note: As a verb; noun form is 'arquivo'

analytics report.note: Fixed from draft's 'relatório de análise': 'relatório analítico' is the more natural adjective-noun pairing used in Brazilian Portuguese BI/reporting contexts

SAN.note: Subject Alternative Name; acronym kept; 'Nome Alternativo de Assunto' is too long for UI

cloud fleet.note: Matches the 'em nuvem' pattern of 'computação em nuvem' (cloud computing), the standard Brazilian Portuguese phrasing

threshold.note: Fixed from draft's 'limiar': 'limite' is the term Brazilian Portuguese monitoring/budget UIs use for a trigger value (e.g. 'limite de orçamento'); 'limiar' is a more academic/psychophysical register (limiar de dor, de ruído) that reads oddly in a budget-alert context

drain.note: As verb; means to let work finish without accepting new work

teardown.note: Fixed from draft's 'desmontagem': matches the term major cloud consoles (AWS/Azure/GCP) use in Brazilian Portuguese for destroying an instance ('encerrar instância'); 'desmontagem' reads as literal mechanical disassembly

webhook.note: Web standard term; universally used in Portuguese technical documentation

branding.note: Could also be 'marca' but 'identidade visual' better captures the concept of app name, colors and logo customization
